doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Beer parties, singing and the bar at the foot of the hill
summary: Fraternity beer parties with group singing, the cheap local bar, and the veterans who set the tone on campus.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: Well you said if you could get ten cents together for a glass of beer. Now where would you go for a glass of beer at Hamilton?

There was a — well remember all of the fraternity houses had bars and there was always a beer party somewhere, or maybe more than one, on Saturday night. And those were pretty much open houses. If it were a closed party I don’t remember that happening a lot but pretty much anyone could come. And the fraternity was — our fraternity whatever — you bought three or four kegs of beer, whatever it was, that’s pretty much all you had, beer. And everybody would come. And what was interesting about this is that what you did very often at these beer parties was sing. In those days everybody sang. People knew how to sing. I’m a terrible singer. Guys in my band won’t even let me sing “Happy Birthday” when we’re asked to do it. But people sang. And you would always find, in any group of people — young people, old people, whatever — people who knew the harmonies to all kinds of songs, Folk songs, pop songs, whatever. So there was a lot more, because you didn’t have so much mechanical music, there was a lot more making of music by human beings in those days than there was, and that goes back to high school. In high school we’d go to a party and people would sing, and that’s what would be happening generally at these beer parties, there’d be a lot of singing, maybe there would be a band, maybe our band would be playing, but mostly not. Bands were too expensive. So that was what people did. So there was a lot of music around. But there was a place down at the foot of the hill — was it called — I can’t remember what it was called — but that was the main place. It was a little bar.

It was a little, like and they had pig’s knuckles in a jar and boiled eggs in a jar, and ten cent beers, and the locals would drink there but a lot of college guys would drink there. The guys who had money would go over to the Alexander Hamilton Inn and drink martinis. But those of us who didn’t have any money, we’d go down there and drink beer. And now you remember, I’m still carrying on about — we should get on to jazz — but see Hamilton was a very different place when I was there. Eighty percent of my freshman class were vets so that what you had at Hamilton at that time was a whole bunch of guys who were older, who had started college and had got drafted and some of these guys were combat veterans, some of these guys were South Pacific veterans and they’d come back and now they’re 22 years old and maybe even married. So they were setting the tone, these older guys. And they weren’t going to have freshman beanies or any of that stuff. That wasn’t going to happen.
They’d wear helmets before that. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-
